validator: draft 1 passes validate.mjs with no hard or soft problems; the faults below are the critic's.
keep: The idea is named up front in two sentences: a polynomial adds up whole-number powers of x [1], and each number that makes it zero gives it a bracket (x − a), lesson 3 run backwards.

The factor theorem is given its cause, not asserted: P(x) = (x − 4)(x² − 2x + 3) + 6 holds for every x, at x = 4 the bracket is 0 so the product is 0, leaving P(4) = 6 as the remainder; a zero remainder means (x − a) divides exactly [2].

Every number is computed and checked: (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, P(4) = 6, P(5) = 24, P(−5) = −336, x³ + 8 = (x + 2)(x² − 2x + 4) with discriminant −12, x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 1)(x − 3)(x + 2), x³ − 3x + 2 = (x − 1)²(x + 2), (5x + 1) ÷ ((x − 1)(x + 2)) = 2 ÷ (x − 1) + 3 ÷ (x + 2), checked at x = 0.

Each lesson-8 misconception in the brief has a DO screen with its own wrong pick: factor against root (screens 2, 6 and 12, the swapped-sign brackets), the factor theorem itself (6, 10), and sign slips in long division (8, whose slip leaves remainder −2 where P(1) = 0 says 0).
Repeated roots touch the axis, with the reason (a square is never negative), tied back to the repeated root of lesson 5; the picture's 'push two handles together' is the brief's own.

Fourteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), end on two mixed puzzles (12, 13), and keep partial fractions to one optional look-ahead screen (14) that says nothing later depends on it.
The analogy (cable drum, off-cut as remainder) is from Dan's trade, reproduces the main result and says where it breaks.
fix: Factual slip: 'x² − 5x + 6 splits into (x − 2)(x − 3) because 2 and 3 add to 5' has the sign wrong. The two numbers are −2 and −3, which add to −5 and multiply to 6.
One name for one thing: P is the polynomial throughout (P(a), P(4)), but the puzzle sentence calls the load's power P = 12I − 0.5I² as well. Write the power rule without the letter P.
Unreadable label: P(x) is used without being introduced in the explanation. Say 'call the rule P(x), so P(4) is its value at x = 4', as in Functions and their graphs.
False absolute in practice: 'The remainder must come out 0' is only true when P(a) = 0. Say so.

False absolute in practice: 'Then the roots are not whole numbers' holds only when every divisor of the plain number has been tried and the x³ has nothing in front with whole numbers throughout. Say 'if none of the plain number's divisors works, it has no whole-number root'.
Causal step skipped: why the remainder is a plain number with no x. Add that the division stops when what is left has no x for the bracket's x to divide into.

Causal step thin: 'the plain number is the root times the plain number of what is left, with a sign' is vague. Show it: (x − a)(x² + bx + c) has plain number −a × c, so a whole-number root a divides it.
Unsourced name dressed as fact: the remainder theorem's name is not in RESEARCH. Say 'textbooks call this the remainder theorem'.
Term order: 'cubic' is used in paragraph 3 before it is explained there; name it where x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 first appears.
ignores: 'a number in front stretches the curve' leaves out that a negative number also flips it. Say 'stretches it, or flips it if negative'.
verdict: rewrite as draft 2 with the fixes above
